doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: What makes a tune worth recording: trio versus dense pieces
summary: Davies says her approach differs by project: simple motifs for the Satori trio, gigging the denser pieces for the Alcyona Mick album before recording. Rowe links 'less is more' to Count Basie.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I see you in a studio setting and I saw a quote from you I’ll start with and I’ll just paraphrase but you were talking about writing tunes and inspiration and that you depend often on your bandmates to make new ideas recordable. And I thought that was an interesting adjective, and what for you makes (now that you’re in the studio recording) what makes a tune or a composition worthy of recording?

Ah. I don’t remember saying that. But I think there were lots of different directions I could go in and I was probably – I would probably answer that differently depending on which project I’m recording. So Satori is my trio, drums, bass, and me. And for that one I would say less is very much more, so I try to write very simple motific themes that we can then develop as a band. So there’s lots of freedom, lots of space. It can go anywhere. So in that sense I’d probably say I won’t want to make something recordable but that we’ll just see what happens in the session. Whereas if the project is either -- the last album I did was with the great English piano player Alcyona Mick. So the tunes that I wrote for that were much more involved, much more harmonically dense, much more complex I suppose. And then I would really want to have a sense of more of the structure in the shape of how it would end up. And I suppose what I meant by that quote might have been more we need to play it in, we need to gig these kind of tunes before we record them so that we’re comfortable with where we could go. Otherwise it’s a bit – you get in that recording mindset of, “Well that wasn’t really the take, let’s do it again, and then you’re trying to find something rather than allow all this spontaneousness, spontaneity let’s say, that comes out of those situations.

That’s a great explanation. And when you said “less is more” it just made an impression on me because over my shoulder is the picture of Count Basie, who that was his mantra for a lot of things, you know with his own playing and the arrangements that he liked, he didn’t want them to be too dense. So you’re after spontaneity with this particular project.
